title: Client, server and host: who asks and who answers

videos.script: You type an address, press enter, and a page appears. It feels like one thing. It is not one thing — it is a conversation, and it has exactly two sides. {{two-sides}} One side asks. The other side answers. That is the whole shape, and everything else in this course is detail hung on it. Here is why it is worth an entire lesson. Almost everyone arriving here already has a picture in their head: a client is a small machine, a server is a big one in a cold room. That picture is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that will cost you later — because it makes the next four lessons look like arbitrary rules instead of consequences. {{wrong-picture}} By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at any exchange on the internet — a page loading, a message sending, a file uploading — and say which side is which, and why it can be the other way round a second later. {{title}} First, the two words everybody uses and almost nobody defines.

Here is one exchange, start to finish. On the left, a browser. On the right, a machine in a data centre. {{scene}} The browser asks: give me the page at this address. It is the client, because it asked. The machine answers with the page. It is the server, because it answered. {{first-exchange}} Now watch what the machine does before it can answer. It does not have the page lying around — it has to build it, and to build it it needs your order history, which lives somewhere else: a database, on a third machine. {{database}} So it asks. And in that instant, the thing we just called a server is a client. Same machine, same second, different role — because the role is the position in an exchange, not a label on a box. {{role-flip}} It asks, the database answers, and only then does it turn back around and answer the browser that has been waiting this whole time. {{return}} Three machines, two exchanges, and the middle one played both parts. If you can see that, you can read the rest of this course.
